# How to use this guide

Pathology I is a third-semester subject of the INC 2021 B.Sc Nursing curriculum. The INC gives it **1 credit (20 hours of theory, which include a few laboratory and visit hours)**. It teaches general pathology (how cells, tissues and organs react to disease), the systemic (special) pathology of common diseases, and the laboratory and blood-bank tests a nurse meets every day. Study it alongside your Adult Health Nursing I pathophysiology, because the two explain the same diseases from different angles.

## This is a "Part I" course — no university exam this semester

**There is no end-semester university theory examination for Pathology I in Semester 3.** Only internal (sessional/college) marks are recorded this semester, and they are **carried forward**. Pathology is examined by the university **together with Pathology II and Genetics (PATH(II)210) in Semester 4**, as one written paper.

In that Semester 4 paper, pathology forms a **section of a combined 3-hour, 75-mark paper** shared with Applied Pharmacology II:

| Section | Subject | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Pharmacology II | 38 |
| B | Pathology (Part I + Part II) | 25 |
| C | Genetics | 12 |

So the pathology you learn now is **not wasted or over by the end of this semester** — it comes back in the Section B pathology questions next semester. Revise it again before the Part II exam. Genetics is taught and examined with Pathology II (Section C); it is **not** part of this Part I course, so it is not covered here.

Because the real exam is next semester, the mock test in this pack is called a **"Practice paper (no university exam this semester)."** It is built in the shape of the **Section B pathology** questions you will meet in Semester 4, so you can test yourself in the right style now.

## How the units are arranged

The INC syllabus for Pathology I has only **three units**, but Unit I and Unit II each pack in many separate topics. To keep every notes file a useful size, the three INC units are **split into eight notes files**:

| Notes file | INC unit | Content covered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 Introduction, cell injury and cellular adaptations | I | Importance and terms of pathology, cell injury, necrosis, gangrene, cellular adaptations, apoptosis |
| Unit 2 Inflammation and wound healing | I | Acute, chronic and granulomatous inflammation; wound healing |
| Unit 3 Neoplasia | I | Nomenclature, normal vs cancer cell, benign vs malignant, carcinoma in situ, metastasis |
| Unit 4 Circulatory disturbances, oedema and body fluids | I | Thrombosis, embolism, shock; oedema; transudate and exudate |
| Unit 5 Special pathology: respiratory and cardiovascular systems | II | Pneumonia, lung abscess, TB, COPD, lung tumours; atherosclerosis, ischaemia/infarction, rheumatic and infective heart disease |
| Unit 6 Special pathology: GIT, liver, gall bladder and pancreas | II | Peptic ulcer, gastritis/H. pylori, oral and GI cancers, typhoid ulcer, IBD; hepatitis, cirrhosis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis |
| Unit 7 Special pathology: skeletal and endocrine systems | II | Bone healing, osteoporosis, osteomyelitis, bone tumours, arthritis; diabetes, goitre, thyroid cancer |
| Unit 8 Haematological tests, blood chemistry and blood bank | III | Hb, cell counts, PCV, ESR; BT, PT, APTT; blood chemistry; blood grouping, components, plasmapheresis, transfusion reactions |

The numbers 1–8 are the StudyDesk unit numbers; the right-hand column shows the matching INC unit. Study one notes file at a sitting: read it, draw each `text` diagram once from memory, then answer that unit's questions and MCQs without looking.

## The practice paper pattern

The practice paper follows the **Section B pathology** style of the Semester 4 combined paper, as given in INC Regulations 2020, Appendix 3. There is **no internal choice** — every question is to be answered. Confirm the exact pattern with your university, as universities print papers differently.

| Part | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MCQ | 4 multiple-choice questions | 4 × 1 = 4 |
| Short | 3 short answers | 3 × 5 = 15 |
| Very short | 3 very short answers | 3 × 2 = 6 |
| **Total** | | **25** |

The pathology section has **no long essay** (the 10-mark essays in that combined paper fall in the pharmacology section), so the practice paper has no essay either. Even so, this pack still gives you long (essay-style) questions in each unit, because learning the full structured answer is the surest way to score in the short answers and in next semester's exam. The practice paper is timed at **60 minutes** (about 2.4 minutes per mark, the usual pace).

A separate **Quick MCQ test (20 questions, 20 minutes)** lets you drill facts fast before a class test or viva.

## Probability ratings

- **High** — a favourite; comes up in most papers in some form. Learn the full answer.
- **Medium** — appears every few papers, or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but worth knowing for MCQs and very short answers.

These ratings are estimates from the weight of each topic in the INC syllabus and the usual style of nursing pathology papers. They are a guide, not a promise of what will be asked.

## Where the marks usually come from

| Notes file | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Reversible vs irreversible cell injury, types of necrosis, dry vs wet gangrene, apoptosis vs necrosis, atrophy/hypertrophy/hyperplasia/metaplasia/dysplasia |
| 2 | Cardinal signs, vascular and cellular events of acute inflammation, acute vs chronic inflammation, granuloma, wound healing (first vs second intention), factors affecting healing |
| 3 | Benign vs malignant tumour, carcinoma in situ, routes of metastasis, grading vs staging |
| 4 | Thrombosis and Virchow's triad, embolism, types of shock, oedema causes, transudate vs exudate |
| 5 | Lobar pneumonia stages, pulmonary TB, COPD types compared, atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, rheumatic heart disease |
| 6 | Gastric vs duodenal ulcer, H. pylori, cirrhosis, viral hepatitis types, Crohn's vs ulcerative colitis |
| 7 | Osteoporosis, osteomyelitis, rheumatoid vs osteoarthritis, diabetes types and complications, goitre |
| 8 | Normal values of Hb/counts/ESR, BT/PT/APTT, ABO and Rh grouping, cross-matching, transfusion reactions and the nurse's role |

## Scoring tips for this subject

1. **Lead every answer with a one-line definition.** Pathology examiners reward a crisp definition of the term before you explain it.
2. **Use the cause → mechanism → changes → effects → nursing frame.** For any disease write aetiology (cause), pathogenesis (how it develops), morphology (the changes), clinical and laboratory features, and a couple of nursing points. This frame fits almost every question.
3. **Comparisons are easy marks — answer them as tables.** Dry vs wet gangrene, apoptosis vs necrosis, acute vs chronic inflammation, benign vs malignant, gastric vs duodenal ulcer, rheumatoid vs osteoarthritis, transudate vs exudate.
4. **Learn the normal laboratory values** from Unit 8 (Hb, TLC, platelets, PCV, ESR, BT, PT, APTT, blood sugar). MCQs and very short answers love them.
5. **Add nursing points.** Every INC unit asks you to apply pathology in nursing — specimen collection, pressure-sore prevention, wound care, diabetic foot care, transfusion safety. One or two lines lift a short answer.
6. **For very short answers (2 marks)** give a one-line definition plus one example or one fact. Do not write a paragraph.
7. **The night before,** read the "Remember" list at the end of each notes file and run the Quick MCQ test.

# Last-night revision sheet

Pathology I is examined with **Pathology II and Genetics next semester** (Section B of the Semester 4 paper), so this revision also sets you up for then. If you have one hour, learn the comparison tables below and the normal laboratory values.

**General pathology — key terms**

| Term | One-line meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Aetiology / pathogenesis | Cause / mechanism of a disease |
| Hypoxia / ischaemia / infarction | Low oxygen / low blood supply / tissue death from lost blood supply |
| Necrosis | Death of groups of cells in a living body (pathological) |
| Apoptosis | Programmed single-cell suicide, no inflammation |
| Atrophy / hypertrophy / hyperplasia | Smaller cells / bigger cells / more cells |
| Metaplasia / dysplasia | One cell type replaced by another / disordered premalignant growth |

**Must-know comparisons**

| Compare | Key difference |
| --- | --- |
| Reversible vs irreversible injury | Reversible = cell swelling, fatty change; irreversible = mitochondrial failure + membrane rupture |
| Coagulative vs liquefactive necrosis | Solid-organ infarcts vs brain infarct and abscess; caseous = TB; fat = pancreatitis |
| Dry vs wet gangrene | Dry: clear demarcation, slow, less toxaemia; wet: no line, fast, severe toxaemia; gas = Clostridium, crepitus |
| Apoptosis vs necrosis | Single cell, energy-needing, no inflammation vs groups of cells, passive, inflammation |
| Acute vs chronic inflammation | Neutrophils, exudate vs macrophages/lymphocytes/plasma cells, fibrosis |
| Transudate vs exudate | Low protein, clear, low SG (<1.012) vs high protein, cloudy, high SG (>1.020), cells |
| Benign vs malignant tumour | Slow, capsulated, no spread vs fast, invasive, metastasises, anaplastic |
| First vs second intention healing | Clean sutured wound, thin scar vs open wound, much granulation, large scar |
| Gastric vs duodenal ulcer | Pain soon after food, weight loss, can be malignant vs pain 2–3 h after/at night, relieved by food, rarely malignant |
| Rheumatoid vs osteoarthritis | Autoimmune, symmetrical small joints, morning stiffness vs wear-and-tear, weight-bearing joints, worse on use |
| Type 1 vs Type 2 diabetes | Young, insulin deficiency, ketosis-prone vs older, insulin resistance, obesity |

**Inflammation — sequences**

```text
Vascular: vasoconstriction → vasodilatation → increased permeability → stasis
Cellular: margination → rolling (selectins) → adhesion (integrins) → emigration → chemotaxis → phagocytosis → killing
```
Histamine = first mediator; C5a and LTB4 = chemotactic; C3b = opsonin; IL-1/TNF/IL-6 = fever and acute-phase response. Granuloma = epithelioid cells + Langhans giant cells + lymphocytes ± caseation (TB).

**Neoplasia**

- Carcinoma = malignant epithelial; sarcoma = malignant connective tissue; -oma usually benign (but melanoma, lymphoma are malignant).
- Carcinoma in situ = full-thickness dysplasia, basement membrane intact (not yet invading).
- Routes of spread: local invasion, lymphatic (carcinomas), blood (sarcomas), transcoelomic (body cavities).
- Grade = how abnormal the cells look; stage (TNM) = how far it has spread — stage matters more for prognosis.

**Circulation and fluids**

- Virchow's triad (thrombosis): endothelial injury, altered blood flow (stasis/turbulence), hypercoagulability.
- Emboli: thromboembolism (commonest), fat, air, amniotic fluid; pulmonary embolism from DVT.
- Shock types: hypovolaemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive. Stages: non-progressive → progressive → irreversible.

**Systemic pathology — one-liners**

| Disease | Remember |
| --- | --- |
| Lobar pneumonia | 4 stages: congestion → red hepatisation → grey hepatisation → resolution |
| Pulmonary TB | Caseating granuloma; Ghon focus + node = Ghon complex; AFB on sputum |
| COPD | Chronic bronchitis (blue bloater, productive cough) + emphysema (pink puffer, air trapping) |
| Atherosclerosis | Lipid plaque in intima; risk: age, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, high LDL |
| Myocardial infarction | Coronary thrombosis; troponin and CK-MB rise; coagulative necrosis |
| Rheumatic heart disease | Follows group A streptococcal sore throat; mitral valve; Aschoff bodies |
| Cirrhosis | Diffuse fibrosis + regenerating nodules; causes alcohol, viral hepatitis |
| Viral hepatitis | A and E faeco-oral; B, C, D blood/body fluids; B and C → chronic, cirrhosis, cancer |
| Osteoporosis | Low bone mass, fragile bones; post-menopausal and senile; fractures of hip, spine, wrist |
| Goitre | Enlarged thyroid; simple (iodine lack) or toxic (Graves' — exophthalmos) |

**Laboratory normal values (adults)**

| Test | Normal (confirm with your lab) |
| --- | --- |
| Haemoglobin | Men ~13–17 g/dL, women ~12–15 g/dL |
| Total leucocyte count | 4,000–11,000 /µL |
| Platelet count | 1.5–4.5 lakh /µL (150,000–450,000) |
| PCV (haematocrit) | Men ~40–50%, women ~36–46% |
| ESR (Westergren) | Men <15 mm/h, women <20 mm/h |
| Bleeding time | 2–7 minutes |
| Prothrombin time | 11–16 seconds (reported with INR) |
| APTT | ~25–35 seconds |
| Fasting blood sugar | 70–100 mg/dL; diabetes ≥126 mg/dL |
| HbA1c | diabetes ≥6.5% |

PT tests the **extrinsic** pathway (warfarin); APTT tests the **intrinsic** pathway (heparin); BT tests platelet and vessel function.

**Blood bank**

- ABO: group A has anti-B, B has anti-A, AB none (universal recipient), O both (universal donor for red cells). Rh-negative mother + Rh-positive baby → haemolytic disease of the newborn.
- Cross-matching before every transfusion. Components: packed red cells, platelets, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate.
- **Acute haemolytic reaction** (ABO mismatch) is the most dangerous: fever, chills, back/loin pain, red urine, fall in blood pressure. **Stop the transfusion first, keep the line open with saline, inform the doctor and blood bank, return the unit.**

**Nursing links to quote**: turn bedridden patients to prevent pressure-sore necrosis; aseptic wound care; protein and vitamin C for healing; diabetic foot inspection to prevent gangrene; correct specimen tube, timing and labelling; identity and cross-match checks and close watch in the first 15 minutes of a transfusion.

**Exam reminder**: Pathology I has no separate university exam — it is examined with Pathology II and Genetics next semester. The practice paper here = 4 MCQ (4) + 3 short (15) + 3 very short (6) = 25 marks, no choice.

# Unit 1: Introduction, cell injury and cellular adaptations

INC Unit I (first part): importance of pathology, common terms, cell injury (causes, reversible and irreversible injury), necrosis, gangrene, cellular adaptations and apoptosis. Inflammation, neoplasia and circulatory disturbances from the same INC unit are in notes files 2, 3 and 4.

## 1.1 What pathology is and why a nurse studies it

**Pathology** (Greek *pathos* = suffering, *logos* = study) is the study of disease: what causes it, how it develops, what it does to cells, tissues and organs, and how these changes produce the signs and symptoms we see at the bedside.

Pathology is the bridge between the basic sciences (anatomy, physiology, biochemistry, microbiology) and clinical nursing. When you know *why* a patient has oedema, *why* a wound is not healing or *why* the haemoglobin is low, your observations become purposeful and your care plan becomes logical.

Why it matters to the nurse:

- **Understanding the disease** — the nurse can explain the condition to the patient and family in simple words.
- **Observation** — knowing the expected course helps you spot complications early (for example, a pale, cold limb after a fracture may mean blocked blood flow).
- **Laboratory work** — nurses collect blood, urine, stool, sputum and body fluids. The right container, timing and labelling decide whether the result is useful. A haemolysed or mislabelled sample can harm a patient.
- **Interpreting reports** — a nurse who understands a raised ESR, a low platelet count or a long prothrombin time knows which precautions to take.
- **Prevention and health education** — knowing risk factors (smoking, alcohol, obesity) lets the nurse teach prevention.

### Branches of pathology

| Branch | What it studies | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General pathology | Basic reactions of cells and tissues common to all diseases | Cell injury, inflammation, healing, neoplasia |
| Systemic (special) pathology | Diseases of each organ system | Pneumonia, peptic ulcer, cirrhosis |
| Histopathology | Tissue changes seen under the microscope | Biopsy of a breast lump |
| Cytopathology | Individual cells shed or aspirated | Pap smear, fine-needle aspiration (FNAC) |
| Haematology | Blood and blood-forming organs | Anaemia, leukaemia, bleeding disorders |
| Clinical pathology | Laboratory tests on body fluids | Urine, stool, CSF examination |
| Chemical pathology (clinical biochemistry) | Chemicals in blood and fluids | Blood sugar, urea, bilirubin |
| Immunopathology | Immune system in disease | Allergy, autoimmunity |
| Forensic pathology | Disease and injury in legal cases | Medicolegal autopsy |

## 1.2 Common terms used in pathology

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Health | A state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease (WHO) |
| Disease | A change from normal structure or function that produces signs or symptoms |
| Aetiology (etiology) | The cause of a disease |
| Pathogenesis | The sequence of events by which the cause produces the disease (the mechanism) |
| Morphology | The structural changes in cells and tissues — gross (naked eye) and microscopic |
| Lesion | Any abnormal change in a tissue caused by disease or injury |
| Symptom | What the patient feels and complains of (pain, nausea) |
| Sign | What the examiner finds (fever, jaundice, enlarged liver) |
| Syndrome | A group of signs and symptoms that occur together |
| Diagnosis | Identifying the disease from history, examination and tests |
| Prognosis | The likely outcome of the disease |
| Complication | A new problem arising during the course of a disease |
| Sequela (plural sequelae) | A lasting after-effect of a disease (deformity after polio) |
| Idiopathic | Cause unknown |
| Iatrogenic | Caused by treatment or a health worker |
| Congenital / acquired | Present at birth / developing later |
| Acute / chronic | Sudden and short / slow and long-lasting |
| Biopsy | Removal of living tissue for examination |
| Autopsy (necropsy) | Examination of the body after death |
| Hypoxia / anoxia | Reduced / absent oxygen supply to tissues |
| Ischaemia | Reduced blood supply to a part |
| Infarction | Death of tissue due to loss of blood supply |

## 1.3 Cell injury: causes (aetiology)

Cells constantly adjust to demands. When a stress is too strong or lasts too long, the cell is **injured**. If the stress stops early, the injury is **reversible**; if it continues, the cell dies (**irreversible injury**).

```text
 Normal cell ──stress──► Adaptation (atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia)
      │
      └── severe stress ──► Reversible injury ──► recovery if cause removed
                                     │
                                     └── continued ──► Irreversible injury ──► cell death
                                                                   (necrosis or apoptosis)
```

Main causes of cell injury:

1. **Hypoxia** — the most common cause. Due to ischaemia (blocked artery), poor oxygenation of blood (respiratory failure), reduced oxygen-carrying capacity (anaemia, carbon monoxide poisoning).
2. **Physical agents** — trauma, extreme heat (burns) or cold (frostbite), electric shock, radiation, sudden changes in atmospheric pressure.
3. **Chemical agents and drugs** — strong acids and alkalis, poisons, alcohol, tobacco smoke, some drugs in excess, even too much glucose or salt.
4. **Infectious agents** — viruses, bacteria (and their toxins), fungi, parasites.
5. **Immunological reactions** — allergy (anaphylaxis) and autoimmune diseases, where the body attacks its own cells.
6. **Genetic defects** — sickle cell anaemia, inborn errors of metabolism.
7. **Nutritional imbalance** — protein–energy malnutrition, vitamin deficiency, and also excess (obesity, high-fat diet leading to atherosclerosis).
8. **Ageing** — reduced capacity of cells to repair themselves.
9. **Psychological factors** — prolonged stress contributes to some diseases.

## 1.4 Pathogenesis: how cells get injured

Different causes act through a few common mechanisms:

| Mechanism | What happens | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ATP depletion | Lack of oxygen stops aerobic respiration; the sodium pump fails, so sodium and water enter the cell and it swells; anaerobic glycolysis produces lactic acid and lowers pH | Ischaemia of heart muscle |
| Mitochondrial damage | Less ATP; leakage of proteins that trigger apoptosis | Hypoxia, toxins |
| Calcium influx | Excess calcium inside the cell activates enzymes that digest membranes, proteins and DNA | Ischaemia, toxins |
| Free radicals (reactive oxygen species) | Unstable oxygen molecules damage lipids of membranes, proteins and DNA | Radiation, reperfusion after ischaemia, chemicals, ageing |
| Membrane damage | Loss of selective permeability; contents leak out | Bacterial toxins, complement |
| DNA and protein damage | Cell triggers apoptosis if repair fails | Radiation, drugs |

### Reversible cell injury

The cell is damaged but recovers if the cause is removed.

- **Cellular swelling (cloudy swelling, hydropic change)** — the earliest change. Pump failure lets water in; the organ looks pale, swollen and heavy.
- **Fatty change (steatosis)** — fat droplets collect in the cytoplasm, mostly in the liver (alcohol, malnutrition, diabetes, obesity). The liver is enlarged, yellow and greasy.
- Other features: loss of microvilli, blebs on the cell surface, swelling of mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum, clumping of nuclear chromatin.

### Irreversible cell injury

Two features mark the "point of no return":

1. Inability to restore mitochondrial function (no ATP even after the oxygen returns).
2. Severe damage to cell membranes, including lysosomal membranes, so enzymes leak and digest the cell.

Clinically, injured cells leak their enzymes into blood. This is the basis of useful tests: cardiac troponins and CK-MB after myocardial infarction, ALT and AST after liver cell injury, amylase and lipase after pancreatic injury.

## 1.5 Necrosis

**Necrosis** is the death of a group of cells or tissue in a living body, followed by breakdown of the dead cells by their own enzymes and by enzymes of white cells. It is always pathological and usually causes inflammation around it.

Nuclear changes in necrosis (seen under the microscope):

- **Pyknosis** — the nucleus shrinks and becomes dark.
- **Karyorrhexis** — the nucleus breaks into fragments.
- **Karyolysis** — the nucleus fades away.

The cytoplasm becomes pink (eosinophilic) because of denatured proteins.

### Types of necrosis

| Type | Mechanism and appearance | Typical site / example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coagulative | Proteins are denatured; outline of dead cells is kept for some days; tissue is firm and pale | Infarcts of heart, kidney, spleen (any solid organ except brain) |
| Liquefactive | Enzymes digest the tissue into a liquid mass | Brain infarct; abscess with pus |
| Caseous | Cheese-like, white, soft, crumbly; a mix of coagulative and liquefactive; surrounded by a granuloma | Tuberculosis |
| Fat necrosis | Fat broken down by lipase; fatty acids combine with calcium to form chalky white spots (saponification) | Acute pancreatitis; injury to the breast |
| Fibrinoid | Protein-like (fibrin) material deposited in damaged vessel walls | Malignant hypertension, vasculitis |
| Gangrenous | Necrosis with putrefaction (see 1.6) | Limbs, bowel |

## 1.6 Gangrene

**Gangrene** is necrosis of a large mass of tissue, usually with added bacterial putrefaction (decay). It commonly affects the limbs, the bowel, the appendix and the gall bladder.

| Feature | Dry gangrene | Wet gangrene | Gas gangrene |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cause | Slow arterial blockage, venous drainage normal | Arterial and venous blockage, or infection of moist tissue | Wound infection with *Clostridium perfringens* and related organisms |
| Common site | Toes, feet (limbs) | Bowel (strangulated hernia, volvulus), diabetic foot, lung | Deep muscle wounds, crushed tissue |
| Appearance | Dry, shrunken, black, mummified | Swollen, soft, moist, foul-smelling | Swollen, crepitus (crackling gas under skin) |
| Line of demarcation | Clear | Poor or absent | Absent |
| Spread | Slow | Rapid | Very rapid |
| Systemic toxicity | Little | Severe (septicaemia) | Severe toxaemia, shock |
| Prognosis | Better | Poor | Poor; an emergency |
| Examples | Atherosclerosis, Buerger's disease, frostbite, ergot | Diabetic foot, strangulated bowel | Road traffic and war wounds |

The black colour comes from iron sulphide formed from haemoglobin breakdown.

## 1.7 Apoptosis

**Apoptosis** ("falling off", like leaves from a tree) is programmed cell death: a controlled, energy-dependent suicide of single cells that removes unwanted cells without inflammation.

Examples:

- **Physiological** — shedding of the endometrium during menstruation, removal of extra cells during embryo development (separation of fingers), death of old neutrophils, removal of self-reactive lymphocytes in the thymus, shrinkage of the breast after weaning.
- **Pathological** — cells with damaged DNA (radiation, anticancer drugs), cells killed by cytotoxic T cells in viral hepatitis, atrophy of an organ after duct obstruction.

Steps: the cell shrinks → chromatin condenses → the cell breaks into membrane-bound pieces (apoptotic bodies) → phagocytes eat them quickly. Enzymes called **caspases** carry out the process.

| Feature | Apoptosis | Necrosis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Number of cells | Single cells | Groups of cells, tissue |
| Cause | Physiological or pathological signals | Always pathological |
| Energy | Needs ATP (active) | Passive |
| Cell size | Shrinks | Swells |
| Cell membrane | Intact | Broken |
| Contents | Packed in apoptotic bodies | Leak out |
| Inflammation | None | Present |
| Nuclear change | Chromatin condensation and fragmentation | Pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis |

Too little apoptosis allows abnormal cells to survive (cancer, autoimmune disease); too much destroys useful cells (neurodegenerative diseases).

## 1.8 Cellular adaptations

Adaptations are reversible changes in the **size, number or type** of cells in response to a changed demand or a stress. They let the cell survive.

```text
 Increased demand ──► Hypertrophy (bigger cells) and/or Hyperplasia (more cells)
 Decreased demand ──► Atrophy (smaller cells)
 Chronic irritation ──► Metaplasia (one adult cell type replaced by another)
 Continued irritation ──► Dysplasia (disordered growth) ──► may become cancer
```

| Adaptation | Definition | Physiological example | Pathological example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Atrophy | Decrease in size of cells and so of the organ | Uterus after delivery; thymus after puberty; ovaries after menopause | Disuse (limb in a plaster cast), denervation (polio), loss of blood supply (brain in old age), malnutrition, pressure (bed sores, tumour pressing on tissue) |
| Hypertrophy | Increase in size of cells and so of the organ, without new cells | Skeletal muscle of athletes; uterus in pregnancy (with hyperplasia) | Left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertension and aortic stenosis |
| Hyperplasia | Increase in the number of cells | Breast at puberty and in pregnancy; liver regeneration after partial removal | Endometrial hyperplasia (excess oestrogen), benign prostatic hyperplasia, warts (viral) |
| Metaplasia | One mature (adult) cell type replaced by another better able to bear the stress | — | Bronchial ciliated columnar → squamous in smokers; squamous → columnar in lower oesophagus with acid reflux (Barrett's oesophagus); cervix (squamous metaplasia) |
| Dysplasia | Disordered growth: cells vary in size and shape, nuclei large and dark, loss of normal layering | — | Cervix (CIN), bronchus of smokers, oral leukoplakia |

Points to note:

- Hypertrophy happens in cells that cannot divide (heart and skeletal muscle); hyperplasia in cells that can divide. Many organs (uterus in pregnancy) show both.
- Metaplasia is protective but loses some function (squamous epithelium in the bronchus has no cilia and no mucus, so clearing of secretions is poorer). If the irritant continues, metaplasia can progress to dysplasia and cancer.
- **Dysplasia is not a true adaptation**; it is a **premalignant** change. Mild dysplasia can revert when the cause is removed; severe dysplasia involving the full thickness of the epithelium is called **carcinoma in situ** (see unit 3).
- **Aplasia** is failure of an organ to develop; **agenesis** is complete absence; **hypoplasia** is incomplete development. These are developmental, not adaptive.

## 1.9 Intracellular accumulations and calcification (short note)

- **Fatty change** (see 1.4) — liver, heart.
- **Pigments** — melanin, haemosiderin (iron, from old bleeding), bilirubin (jaundice), lipofuscin ("wear-and-tear" pigment in old age).
- **Pathological calcification**:
  - **Dystrophic** — calcium deposited in dead or damaged tissue with normal blood calcium (caseous TB, atheroma, damaged heart valves).
  - **Metastatic** — calcium deposited in normal tissues because blood calcium is high (hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, bone destruction by tumour).

## 1.10 Application in nursing

- **Prevent hypoxic injury**: keep the airway clear, give prescribed oxygen, position the breathless patient upright, and watch colour, SpO2 and level of consciousness.
- **Pressure injury (bed sore)**: prolonged pressure causes ischaemia and necrosis. Turn bedridden patients regularly, keep skin clean and dry, use pressure-relieving mattresses and check bony prominences daily.
- **Disuse atrophy**: encourage early mobilisation and active or passive range-of-motion exercises for patients on bed rest or in casts.
- **Diabetic foot care**: daily inspection, proper footwear, nail care and early reporting of colour change prevent gangrene. Teach the patient to recognise dry and wet gangrene.
- **Gas gangrene**: deep, dirty wounds need thorough cleaning; report swelling, crackling under the skin and a foul smell at once.
- **Cancer screening**: metaplasia and dysplasia are warning signs. Encourage women for cervical screening and smokers to quit.
- **Enzyme tests**: understand that troponin, ALT/AST and amylase rise because injured cells leak them; collect samples at the right times.
- **Burns, frostbite, radiation**: these physical agents injure cells directly; protect skin and keep the area clean.

## Remember

- Aetiology = cause; pathogenesis = mechanism; morphology = structural change; prognosis = outcome.
- Hypoxia is the commonest cause of cell injury; ATP depletion → Na+ pump failure → cell swelling.
- Earliest reversible change: cellular swelling. Fatty change is reversible, commonly in the liver.
- Point of no return: mitochondrial failure + membrane damage.
- Nuclear changes of necrosis: pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis.
- Coagulative = infarcts of heart/kidney; liquefactive = brain and abscess; caseous = TB; fat = pancreatitis.
- Dry gangrene: clear line of demarcation, slow, better prognosis; wet gangrene: no line, fast, toxaemia.
- Gas gangrene: *Clostridium perfringens*, crepitus.
- Apoptosis: single cells, energy-dependent, no inflammation, apoptotic bodies, caspases.
- Atrophy ↓ size; hypertrophy ↑ size; hyperplasia ↑ number; metaplasia = change of cell type; dysplasia = premalignant disorder.
- Smoker's bronchus: columnar → squamous metaplasia; Barrett's oesophagus: squamous → columnar.

# Unit 2: Inflammation and wound healing

INC Unit I (second part): acute inflammation (vascular and cellular events, systemic effects), chronic inflammation (granulomatous inflammation, systemic effects) and wound healing.

## 2.1 Definition and purpose

**Inflammation** is the protective response of living vascularised tissue to injury. It brings fluid, proteins and white blood cells from the blood to the site of injury to destroy or wall off the cause, remove dead tissue and start repair.

- It is a **defence**, not a disease in itself. Without it, infections would spread and wounds would not heal.
- It can also **harm**: swelling of the larynx can block the airway; inflammation of the brain or its coverings is dangerous; long-lasting inflammation scars organs (rheumatoid arthritis, cirrhosis).
- The suffix **"-itis"** means inflammation: appendicitis, hepatitis, gastritis.

Causes: infection (the most common), trauma, burns, chemicals, dead tissue (infarct), foreign bodies (sutures, splinters) and immune reactions (allergy, autoimmune disease).

**Inflammation is not the same as infection.** Infection means microbes are present and multiplying; inflammation is the tissue's response, which may or may not be due to microbes (a sprained ankle is inflamed but not infected).

## 2.2 Cardinal signs

| Sign | Latin | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Redness | Rubor | Dilatation of small vessels, more blood in the area |
| Heat | Calor | Increased blood flow |
| Swelling | Tumor | Fluid and cells leaving the vessels (exudate) |
| Pain | Dolor | Mediators (bradykinin, prostaglandins) and stretching of tissue |
| Loss of function | Functio laesa | Pain and swelling limit movement (added by Virchow) |

The first four were described by Celsus.

## 2.3 Acute inflammation

Acute inflammation is rapid in onset (seconds to minutes), lasts a few hours to a few days, and is marked by **fluid exudation** and **neutrophils**.

### A. Vascular events

```text
 Injury
   │
   ▼
 1. Transient vasoconstriction of arterioles (seconds)
   │
   ▼
 2. Vasodilatation (histamine, nitric oxide) → more blood flow → redness, heat
   │
   ▼
 3. Increased vascular permeability (gaps between endothelial cells)
    → protein-rich fluid leaks into tissue → swelling (exudate)
   │
   ▼
 4. Slowing of blood flow (stasis); blood becomes thicker as fluid leaves
   │
   ▼
 5. White cells move to the edge of the vessel → cellular events begin
```

Mechanisms of increased permeability:

- Contraction of endothelial cells creating gaps (histamine, bradykinin) — fast and short-lived; mainly in venules.
- Direct injury to endothelium (burns, toxins) — immediate and lasting.
- Delayed leakage hours later (sunburn, mild heat).
- Leakage through new blood vessels during repair.

### B. Cellular events (leucocyte events)

Neutrophils arrive first (within hours); monocytes/macrophages follow after 24–48 hours.

```text
 Margination ──► Rolling ──► Adhesion ──► Emigration (diapedesis)
      ──► Chemotaxis ──► Phagocytosis ──► Killing and degradation
```

1. **Margination** — as flow slows, white cells move from the centre of the stream to the vessel wall.
2. **Rolling** — they tumble along the endothelium, loosely held by adhesion molecules called **selectins**.
3. **Adhesion (pavementing)** — they stick firmly through **integrins** on the leucocytes binding to molecules on the endothelium.
4. **Emigration (transmigration, diapedesis)** — they squeeze between endothelial cells and cross the basement membrane into the tissue. Red cells may escape passively through the damaged wall (diapedesis of red cells).
5. **Chemotaxis** — they move towards the site of injury, attracted by chemicals (bacterial products, complement C5a, leukotriene B4, chemokines such as IL-8).
6. **Phagocytosis** — recognition and attachment (helped by **opsonins** — antibodies and complement C3b coating the microbe), engulfment into a phagosome, which fuses with a lysosome.
7. **Killing** — by oxygen-dependent mechanisms (reactive oxygen species, the "respiratory burst"; myeloperoxidase forming hypochlorite) and oxygen-independent mechanisms (lysozyme, lactoferrin, defensins).

### C. Chemical mediators (in brief)

| Mediator | Source | Main effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Histamine | Mast cells, basophils, platelets | Vasodilatation, increased permeability (first mediator released) |
| Serotonin | Platelets | Permeability (like histamine) |
| Prostaglandins | Cell membranes (cyclo-oxygenase pathway) | Vasodilatation, pain, fever |
| Leukotrienes | Lipoxygenase pathway | Permeability, bronchospasm, chemotaxis (LTB4) |
| Bradykinin | Plasma (kinin system) | Pain, permeability, vasodilatation |
| Complement (C3a, C5a, C3b) | Plasma | Chemotaxis, opsonisation, mast cell release; C5b–C9 lyses microbes |
| Cytokines (IL-1, TNF, IL-6) | Macrophages, lymphocytes | Fever, acute-phase response, endothelial activation |
| Nitric oxide | Endothelium, macrophages | Vasodilatation, killing of microbes |

Anti-inflammatory drugs act on some of these (for example, aspirin and similar drugs block prostaglandin formation; antihistamines block histamine).

### D. Exudate and its types

The fluid that collects in inflamed tissue is an **exudate** — rich in protein and cells (compare transudate in unit 4).

| Type | Content | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Serous | Thin, watery, little protein | Blister of a burn, early pleural effusion |
| Fibrinous | Rich in fibrin | Fibrinous pericarditis ("bread-and-butter" appearance), lobar pneumonia |
| Suppurative (purulent) | Pus: dead neutrophils, bacteria, debris | Abscess, boil, empyema |
| Haemorrhagic | Many red cells | Severe injury of vessels |
| Catarrhal | Mucus on a mucous membrane | Common cold |
| Pseudomembranous | Membrane of fibrin and dead cells | Diphtheria, antibiotic-associated colitis |

- **Abscess** — a localised collection of pus walled off by a pyogenic membrane (boil, liver abscess).
- **Cellulitis** — diffuse spreading inflammation in loose tissue, usually streptococcal.
- **Ulcer** — loss of surface epithelium with inflammation of the base (peptic ulcer, pressure ulcer).

### E. Systemic effects of acute inflammation (acute-phase response)

Caused mainly by cytokines IL-1, TNF and IL-6.

- **Fever** — cytokines raise prostaglandin production in the hypothalamus and reset the body's thermostat.
- **Leucocytosis** — raised white cell count. Neutrophilia in bacterial infection; lymphocytosis in viral infection; eosinophilia in allergy and worm infestation. **Shift to the left** = more young (band) neutrophils. Some infections (typhoid, some viral infections) cause leucopenia.
- **Acute-phase proteins** made by the liver: C-reactive protein (CRP), fibrinogen, serum amyloid A. Raised fibrinogen makes red cells clump and settle faster — hence a **raised ESR**.
- Other effects: raised pulse, rigors (shivering), loss of appetite, malaise, sleepiness.
- In severe infection: **sepsis and septic shock** — fall in blood pressure, poor organ perfusion (see unit 4).

### F. Outcomes of acute inflammation

```text
                      ┌─► Resolution (complete return to normal) — mild injury, little damage
 Acute inflammation ──┼─► Abscess / suppuration — pyogenic organisms
                      ├─► Healing by fibrosis (scar) — much tissue destruction
                      └─► Chronic inflammation — cause persists
                          (also: spread to lymph nodes and blood → septicaemia)
```

## 2.4 Chronic inflammation

Chronic inflammation lasts weeks to months or years. Inflammation, tissue destruction and attempts at repair go on **at the same time**.

Causes:

- Persistent infection by organisms that resist killing (tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis, fungi).
- Prolonged exposure to toxic agents (silica, asbestos, tobacco smoke, cholesterol in atherosclerosis).
- Autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease).
- Repeated attacks of acute inflammation (recurrent cholecystitis).

Features:

- Infiltration by **mononuclear cells** — macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells.
- **Tissue destruction** caused by the persisting agent and by the inflammatory cells.
- **Repair** — new small blood vessels (angiogenesis) and **fibrosis** (scar).

### Acute versus chronic inflammation

| Feature | Acute | Chronic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Sudden | Slow, or follows acute |
| Duration | Hours to days | Weeks to years |
| Main cells | Neutrophils | Macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells |
| Vascular change | Marked (exudate, oedema) | Less; new vessel formation |
| Tissue damage | Usually mild, self-limited | Progressive |
| Fibrosis | Little | Marked |
| Signs | Prominent | Less obvious |

### Granulomatous inflammation

A special type of chronic inflammation in which activated macrophages collect to form small nodules called **granulomas**.

```text
            Lymphocytes (outer cuff)
        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
        │   Epithelioid cells          │
        │   (activated macrophages)    │
        │      ┌──────────────┐        │
        │      │  Caseous     │  Giant │
        │      │  necrosis    │  cell  │
        │      │  (centre)    │(Langhans)
        │      └──────────────┘        │
        └──────────────────────────────┘
              Fibroblasts and fibrosis (outermost, later)
     Tubercle: a caseating granuloma of tuberculosis
```

Parts of a granuloma: **epithelioid cells** (modified macrophages), **multinucleated giant cells** (Langhans type in TB — nuclei arranged like a horseshoe at the edge; foreign-body type — nuclei scattered), a collar of **lymphocytes**, and **fibrosis** around it. In TB the centre shows **caseous necrosis**.

Causes of granulomas:

- **Infections**: tuberculosis (caseating), leprosy, syphilis (gumma), fungal infections, cat-scratch disease.
- **Foreign bodies**: sutures, talc, silica.
- **Unknown cause**: sarcoidosis (non-caseating), Crohn's disease.

### Systemic effects of chronic inflammation

- Low-grade fever, weight loss, tiredness, loss of appetite.
- **Anaemia of chronic disease** (iron cannot be used properly).
- Raised ESR; raised immunoglobulins (plasma cells).
- **Secondary (reactive) amyloidosis** — abnormal protein deposited in kidney, liver, spleen after long-standing disease (TB, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic osteomyelitis, bronchiectasis).
- Organ scarring and loss of function (cirrhosis, pulmonary fibrosis).

## 2.5 Wound healing (repair)

**Repair** is the restoration of injured tissue. It happens in two ways:

1. **Regeneration** — dead cells are replaced by the same type of cell, restoring normal structure. Possible only in tissues whose cells can divide.
2. **Healing by fibrosis (scar formation)** — dead tissue is replaced by connective tissue when regeneration is not possible or damage is extensive.

### Cells by their ability to divide

| Type | Description | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Labile (continuously dividing) | Divide throughout life | Skin epidermis, lining of gut, bone marrow cells |
| Stable (quiescent) | Normally resting but divide when injured | Liver, kidney tubules, pancreas, fibroblasts, smooth muscle |
| Permanent (non-dividing) | Cannot divide after birth | Neurons, cardiac muscle, (most) skeletal muscle |

That is why a heart infarct heals by a scar, while the liver can regenerate.

### Granulation tissue

The key tissue of repair. Pink, soft, granular and bleeds easily. Made of:

- New capillaries (angiogenesis) that give the granular appearance.
- Fibroblasts that make collagen.
- Inflammatory cells (macrophages).
- Oedema fluid.

With time, collagen increases, vessels decrease, and granulation tissue matures into a pale **scar**.

### Phases of wound healing

```text
 Haemostasis (minutes) → Inflammation (days 1–3) → Proliferation (day 3 to ~3 weeks)
                                          → Maturation / remodelling (3 weeks to 1–2 years)
```

1. **Haemostasis** — vessel constriction, platelet plug and clot; the clot forms a scab.
2. **Inflammation** — neutrophils clean bacteria, then macrophages remove debris and release growth factors.
3. **Proliferation** — granulation tissue fills the defect; epithelium grows in from the edges; **wound contraction** by myofibroblasts reduces the size of the wound.
4. **Maturation (remodelling)** — collagen is rearranged and cross-linked; the scar becomes paler and stronger. A scar never regains full strength — it reaches about 70–80% of normal skin strength.

### Healing by first and second intention

| Feature | First (primary) intention | Second (secondary) intention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wound | Clean, edges brought together (surgical incision with sutures) | Large, gaping, edges apart, often infected, tissue lost (ulcer, abscess cavity, burns) |
| Clot and inflammation | Small | Large |
| Granulation tissue | Little | Abundant, fills from the base upward |
| Wound contraction | Minimal | Marked |
| Healing time | Short | Long |
| Scar | Thin, neat | Large, may be deforming |
| Infection risk | Low | Higher |

**Delayed primary closure (third intention)**: a contaminated wound is left open for a few days, cleaned, and then sutured.

Timeline of a clean sutured incision: the gap fills with clot on day 1; neutrophils appear; epithelium bridges the surface by about 24–48 hours; granulation tissue by day 3; collagen bridges the incision by day 5; by the end of the second week inflammation settles and blanching begins; strength increases over months.

### Factors affecting wound healing

| Local factors | Systemic factors |
| --- | --- |
| Infection (the single most important cause of delay) | Age (slower in the elderly) |
| Poor blood supply (atherosclerosis, varicose veins) | Malnutrition — protein, vitamin C (collagen formation), zinc |
| Foreign bodies (dirt, sutures) | Diabetes mellitus |
| Movement and mechanical stress on the wound | Steroid therapy (reduces inflammation and collagen formation) |
| Size, location and type of wound | Anaemia and poor oxygenation |
| Haematoma and dead tissue | Obesity, smoking, jaundice, uraemia, cancer, radiation |
| Pressure (bed sores) | Immunosuppression |

### Complications of wound healing

- **Wound infection** and dehiscence (wound bursting open, often from infection, poor nutrition or raised abdominal pressure).
- **Hypertrophic scar** — raised, red scar that stays within the wound edges.
- **Keloid** — excess collagen that grows **beyond** the wound edges; more common in dark-skinned people; often recurs after removal.
- **Contracture** — scar contraction limits movement, especially across joints after burns.
- **Incisional hernia**, painful scar (neuroma), implantation cyst, rarely malignant change in a long-standing scar or ulcer (Marjolin's ulcer).

### Healing in specific tissues (in brief)

- **Bone** — callus formation (see unit 7).
- **Nerve** — peripheral nerve can regenerate along its sheath slowly; brain and spinal cord form a glial scar.
- **Heart** — infarct replaced by a fibrous scar.
- **Liver** — regeneration if the framework is intact; scarring in cirrhosis.

## 2.6 Application in nursing

- **Assess inflammation**: look for the five cardinal signs; record temperature, pulse and the size of swelling; mark the edge of cellulitis with a pen to see whether it spreads.
- **Fever care**: tepid sponging, fluids, light clothing, rest, monitoring, and prescribed antipyretics; record the fever chart pattern.
- **Laboratory support**: collect blood for total and differential count, ESR and CRP; send pus or swabs for culture **before** the first antibiotic dose when possible.
- **Abscess**: prepare for incision and drainage; follow aseptic dressing technique; observe drainage amount and colour.
- **Wound care**: aseptic technique and hand hygiene; keep the wound clean, moist and protected; observe for redness, warmth, discharge, smell, separation of edges; remove sutures as ordered.
- **Promote healing**: protein- and vitamin C-rich diet, good glycaemic control in diabetes, stop smoking, mobilise early but splint the wound, prevent pressure.
- **Burns**: watch for contractures; position and exercise joints; pressure garments as advised.
- **Health education**: complete prescribed treatment for TB; explain that steroids can mask signs of infection and slow healing.

## Remember

- Cardinal signs: rubor, calor, tumor, dolor, functio laesa.
- Vascular events: brief vasoconstriction → vasodilatation → increased permeability → stasis.
- Cellular events: margination → rolling (selectins) → adhesion (integrins) → emigration → chemotaxis → phagocytosis → killing.
- Histamine is the first mediator; C5a and LTB4 are chemotactic; C3b is an opsonin; IL-1/TNF cause fever.
- Acute = neutrophils; chronic = macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells.
- Granuloma = epithelioid cells + giant cells + lymphocytes ± caseation (TB) — Langhans giant cell.
- Systemic acute: fever, leucocytosis, raised CRP and ESR. Chronic: anaemia, amyloidosis, weight loss.
- Labile, stable, permanent cells — heart and neurons cannot regenerate.
- Granulation tissue = new capillaries + fibroblasts + inflammatory cells.
- First intention: clean sutured wound, thin scar; second intention: open wound, much granulation and contraction.
- Infection is the commonest local cause of delayed healing; vitamin C and protein are needed for collagen.
- Keloid grows beyond the wound margin; hypertrophic scar does not.

# Unit 3: Neoplasia

INC Unit I (third part): nomenclature of tumours, normal versus cancer cells, benign and malignant tumours, carcinoma in situ, and tumour metastasis — general mechanism, routes of spread with examples of each. Causes, grading, staging and the nurse's role are added because they are needed to answer questions on this topic.

## 3.1 Definitions

- **Neoplasia** means "new growth". A **neoplasm (tumour)** is an abnormal mass of tissue whose growth is excessive, uncoordinated with the normal tissue, and continues even after the stimulus that started it has stopped.
- **Tumour** originally meant any swelling; today it is used for a neoplasm.
- **Cancer** is the common term for all **malignant** tumours (Latin *cancer* = crab, because the tumour sends claw-like extensions into tissue).
- **Oncology** is the study of tumours.

How a neoplasm differs from hyperplasia: hyperplasia is a controlled response that stops when the stimulus stops; a neoplasm is **autonomous** — it keeps growing on its own.

Every tumour has two parts:

1. **Parenchyma** — the tumour cells themselves; they decide the behaviour and the name.
2. **Stroma** — supporting connective tissue and blood vessels. A tumour with much fibrous stroma is hard (scirrhous), as in many breast cancers.

## 3.2 Nomenclature (naming tumours)

The name depends on the **tissue of origin** and whether the tumour is **benign or malignant**.

| Tissue of origin | Benign (suffix "-oma") | Malignant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surface epithelium (squamous) | Squamous cell papilloma | Squamous cell carcinoma |
| Glandular epithelium | Adenoma | Adenocarcinoma |
| Fibrous tissue | Fibroma | Fibrosarcoma |
| Fat | Lipoma | Liposarcoma |
| Cartilage | Chondroma | Chondrosarcoma |
| Bone | Osteoma | Osteosarcoma |
| Smooth muscle | Leiomyoma (fibroid of uterus) | Leiomyosarcoma |
| Skeletal muscle | Rhabdomyoma | Rhabdomyosarcoma |
| Blood vessels | Haemangioma | Angiosarcoma |
| Melanocytes | Naevus (mole) | Malignant melanoma |
| Blood-forming cells | — | Leukaemia, lymphoma |
| Germ cells | Mature teratoma (dermoid cyst) | Seminoma, immature teratoma |

Rules to remember:

- **Carcinoma** = malignant tumour of **epithelial** origin (skin, linings, glands). This is the most common cancer in adults.
- **Sarcoma** = malignant tumour of **mesenchymal** (connective tissue) origin — bone, cartilage, fat, muscle, vessels.
- **Exceptions** — some names end in "-oma" but are malignant: **lymphoma, melanoma, seminoma, hepatoma (hepatocellular carcinoma), mesothelioma, glioma**.
- Some "-omas" are not tumours at all: **haematoma** (collection of blood), **granuloma** (inflammation), **hamartoma** (disorganised mass of normal tissue native to the site, such as some lung nodules).
- **Choristoma** — normal tissue in an abnormal place (pancreatic tissue in the stomach wall).
- **Teratoma** — a tumour containing tissues from all three germ layers (skin, hair, teeth, cartilage), usually in the ovary or testis.
- **Blastoma** — tumours of embryonic tissue, mostly in children: retinoblastoma, nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour), neuroblastoma.

## 3.3 Normal cell versus cancer cell

| Feature | Normal cell | Cancer cell |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Growth control | Divides only when needed; stops on contact with neighbours (contact inhibition) | Divides without control; no contact inhibition |
| Differentiation | Mature, specialised, does its normal job | Poorly differentiated or undifferentiated; loses normal function |
| Size and shape | Uniform | Varies (pleomorphism) |
| Nucleus | Normal size; nuclear : cytoplasmic ratio about 1 : 4–1 : 6 | Large, dark (hyperchromatic), N : C ratio towards 1 : 1, prominent nucleoli |
| Mitosis | Few, normal | Many, some abnormal (tripolar, bizarre) |
| Lifespan | Limited; undergoes apoptosis | Escapes apoptosis; effectively immortal (telomerase active) |
| Adhesion | Cells stick together | Less adhesion; cells break away |
| Invasion | Stays within its basement membrane | Breaks through basement membrane, invades, spreads |
| Chromosomes | Normal number | Often abnormal (aneuploidy) |
| Blood supply | Normal | Stimulates new vessels (angiogenesis) |
| Immune recognition | Recognised as self | May show new antigens but evades the immune system |

**Anaplasia** means lack of differentiation — a hallmark of malignancy. The less a tumour cell resembles its parent cell, the more aggressive it usually is.

## 3.4 Benign versus malignant tumours

| Feature | Benign | Malignant |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Differentiation | Well differentiated, resembles parent tissue | Variable; may be anaplastic |
| Rate of growth | Slow; may stop | Usually rapid |
| Mode of growth | Expansion, pushes tissue aside | Infiltration and invasion of surrounding tissue |
| Capsule | Usually encapsulated | Not encapsulated, irregular edges |
| Mitoses | Few, normal | Many, abnormal |
| Necrosis and haemorrhage | Rare | Common (growth outruns blood supply) |
| Metastasis | **Never** | **Common** — the most reliable sign of malignancy |
| Recurrence after removal | Rare | Common |
| Effect on the patient | Usually local pressure; rarely fatal unless in a vital site (brain) or producing hormones | Cachexia, organ failure, often fatal if untreated |
| Example | Lipoma, fibroadenoma breast, leiomyoma uterus | Carcinoma breast, osteosarcoma, leukaemia |

## 3.5 Dysplasia and carcinoma in situ

```text
 Normal epithelium → Metaplasia → Mild dysplasia → Moderate → Severe dysplasia
                                    (lower 1/3)     (2/3)        (full thickness)
                                                                   │
                                                  Carcinoma in situ (CIS)
                                                  basement membrane INTACT
                                                                   │
                                                  Invasive carcinoma
                                                  basement membrane BREACHED → can spread
```

- **Dysplasia** — disordered growth of epithelium with abnormal cells (variation in size and shape, large dark nuclei, more mitoses, loss of layering). Can regress if the cause is removed.
- **Carcinoma in situ (CIS)** — malignant-looking cells involve the **whole thickness** of the epithelium but have **not broken through the basement membrane**. Because there are no blood vessels or lymphatics in the epithelium, CIS **cannot metastasise** and is curable by complete removal.
- Common sites: cervix (cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN III), skin, oral cavity, breast ducts (ductal CIS), bronchus.
- Once the cells invade through the basement membrane, it is **invasive (frank) carcinoma**.

This is the scientific basis of **screening**: detecting dysplasia or CIS (for example by a Pap smear or visual inspection with acetic acid for the cervix) allows cure before invasion.

## 3.6 Causes (carcinogenesis) — in brief

Cancer results from accumulated **mutations** in genes that control cell growth:

- **Oncogenes** (activated growth-promoting genes) — act like a stuck accelerator.
- **Tumour suppressor genes** lost or inactivated (p53, RB) — act like failed brakes.
- Genes of DNA repair and apoptosis.

Carcinogens (agents that cause cancer):

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| Chemical | Tobacco smoke and chewing tobacco (lung, mouth, bladder), aflatoxin from mouldy grains (liver), asbestos (mesothelioma), benzene (leukaemia), aniline dyes (bladder), alcohol |
| Physical | Ultraviolet light (skin), ionising radiation (leukaemia, thyroid) |
| Viral | Human papillomavirus (cervix, oral), hepatitis B and C (liver), Epstein–Barr virus (Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma), HIV (Kaposi sarcoma, lymphomas), HTLV-1 |
| Bacterial | *Helicobacter pylori* (stomach cancer, gastric lymphoma) |
| Hereditary | BRCA1/BRCA2 (breast, ovary), familial polyposis (colon), retinoblastoma |
| Hormonal | Unopposed oestrogen (endometrium) |

Carcinogenesis occurs in steps: **initiation** (irreversible DNA damage) → **promotion** (repeated stimulation of the damaged cells to divide) → **progression** (more mutations, invasion and spread).

## 3.7 Tumour metastasis

**Metastasis** is the spread of tumour cells from the primary site to distant tissues, where they form secondary tumours not connected to the original one. It is the single most reliable feature of malignancy and the main cause of cancer death.

### General mechanism (invasion–metastasis cascade)

```text
 1. Detachment: cancer cells lose adhesion molecules (E-cadherin) and separate
 2. Invasion: enzymes (collagenases, metalloproteinases) digest the basement membrane
    and the matrix; cells move into the stroma
 3. Intravasation: cells enter lymphatics or blood vessels
 4. Survival in circulation: cells travel alone or as clumps with platelets
 5. Arrest and extravasation: cells stick to the vessel wall of a distant organ and leave the vessel
 6. Colonisation: cells multiply and stimulate new blood vessels (angiogenesis)
    → secondary tumour (metastasis)
```

Most cancer cells that enter the blood die; only a few succeed. Some organs are common targets because of blood flow pattern (the lungs and liver filter blood) and "soil" suitability.

### Routes of spread

| Route | How | Typical examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Direct (local) invasion | Grows into neighbouring tissues | Cervical carcinoma into bladder and rectum; oral cancer into the jaw |
| 2. Lymphatic spread | Cells enter lymphatics and reach regional lymph nodes, which become enlarged, hard and matted | **Carcinomas** usually: breast cancer → axillary nodes; stomach cancer → left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node, Troisier's sign); lung cancer → hilar nodes |
| 3. Haematogenous (blood) spread | Cells enter veins (thin walls) | **Sarcomas** usually; also some carcinomas. Via **portal vein → liver** (colorectal, stomach, pancreas cancers); via **systemic veins → lungs** (sarcomas, kidney cancer); via vertebral veins → spine (prostate cancer); renal cell carcinoma grows into the renal vein; hepatocellular carcinoma into hepatic veins |
| 4. Transcoelomic spread (across body cavities) | Cells fall into the peritoneal, pleural or pericardial cavity and seed its surface | Ovarian cancer spreads throughout the peritoneum (malignant ascites); gastric cancer to both ovaries (**Krukenberg tumour**); lung cancer → pleural effusion |
| 5. Implantation | Cells carried mechanically | Along a needle biopsy tract, surgical wound, instruments; along the CSF (medulloblastoma) |

Common sites of metastasis: **lymph nodes, liver, lungs, bone, brain**. Cancers that commonly spread to bone: breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid. Prostate cancer deposits in bone are typically bone-forming (osteoblastic); most others destroy bone (osteolytic) and raise blood calcium.

## 3.8 Grading and staging

- **Grading** is based on the microscopic appearance — how differentiated the cells are and how many mitoses. Grade I (well differentiated) to Grade III or IV (poorly differentiated/anaplastic). A higher grade usually means more aggressive behaviour.
- **Staging** describes how far the cancer has spread; it predicts outcome better than grade. The common system is **TNM**:
  - **T** — size and local extent of the primary tumour (T0–T4; Tis = carcinoma in situ).
  - **N** — regional lymph node involvement (N0–N3).
  - **M** — distant metastasis (M0 absent, M1 present).

## 3.9 Effects of tumours on the patient

- **Local effects**: pressure (brain tumour raises intracranial pressure), obstruction (bowel, bile duct causing jaundice, bronchus causing collapse), ulceration and bleeding, pain, pathological fracture.
- **Cancer cachexia**: loss of appetite, weight and muscle, weakness — caused by cytokines (TNF) and tumour products.
- **Anaemia**: chronic blood loss, marrow replacement, poor nutrition.
- **Infections**: reduced immunity, especially in leukaemia and during chemotherapy.
- **Hormone production**: functional tumours (insulinoma causing low blood sugar).
- **Paraneoplastic syndromes**: effects not explained by local or metastatic spread — high calcium, Cushing's syndrome from lung cancer, increased clotting (migratory thrombophlebitis).

## 3.10 Laboratory diagnosis of tumours (overview)

- **Histopathology** — biopsy (incisional, excisional, needle core); the definitive diagnosis. Fixed in 10% formalin.
- **Frozen section** — rapid report during surgery.
- **Cytology** — exfoliative (Pap smear, sputum, fluids) and fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC).
- **Immunohistochemistry** — identifies cell type using antibodies.
- **Tumour markers** in blood (help monitoring, rarely diagnose alone): alpha-fetoprotein (liver cancer, germ-cell tumours), CEA (colorectal), PSA (prostate), CA-125 (ovary), beta-hCG (choriocarcinoma, testicular tumours).
- Imaging (X-ray, ultrasound, CT, MRI) and endoscopy locate the tumour.

## 3.11 Application in nursing

- **Early warning signs of cancer** to teach the public (commonly summarised as "CAUTION"): Change in bowel or bladder habits; A sore that does not heal; Unusual bleeding or discharge; Thickening or lump in the breast or elsewhere; Indigestion or difficulty swallowing; Obvious change in a wart or mole; Nagging cough or hoarseness.
- **Prevention**: stop tobacco in all forms and limit alcohol; healthy diet and weight; HPV and hepatitis B vaccination as per national schedules; protection from occupational carcinogens.
- **Screening**: oral visual examination, breast self- and clinical examination, cervical screening; India's national programme for non-communicable diseases includes screening for oral, breast and cervical cancer — check the current guidelines of the Ministry of Health for age groups.
- **Specimen handling**: biopsy into adequate formalin (about ten times the tissue volume), labelled with name, site and date; send with a request form and relevant history.
- **Patient care**: emotional support at diagnosis; nutrition for cachexia; infection prevention in low white cell counts; pain assessment; care of pathological fracture risk in bone metastasis.
- **Observation for complications**: signs of raised intracranial pressure, obstruction, bleeding, and confusion or constipation from high calcium.

## Remember

- Neoplasm = autonomous, excessive growth that continues after the stimulus stops.
- Benign "-oma"; malignant epithelial = carcinoma; malignant connective tissue = sarcoma.
- Malignant despite "-oma": lymphoma, melanoma, seminoma, hepatoma, mesothelioma, glioma.
- Hamartoma = disorganised native tissue; choristoma = normal tissue in the wrong place.
- Anaplasia = loss of differentiation; pleomorphism, hyperchromasia, high N : C ratio, abnormal mitoses.
- Metastasis is the most reliable sign of malignancy; benign tumours never metastasise.
- CIS: full-thickness atypia, basement membrane intact, cannot metastasise.
- Carcinomas → lymphatics; sarcomas → blood.
- Gastrointestinal cancers → liver (portal vein); sarcomas → lungs.
- Krukenberg tumour = ovarian metastasis from stomach; Virchow's node = left supraclavicular.
- Grade = microscopic differentiation; stage = spread (TNM). Stage matters more for prognosis.
